What type of epilepsy do you have?

I have a generalized genetic-type of epilepsy which causes tonic-clonic seizures (the kind of seizures you typically think of when talking about epilepsy). I was initially diagnosed with juvenile myclonic epilepsy, but the neurologists have since changed their minds to just 'genetically-based.'

How has it affected your life?

It has affected my life in many ways. Most greatly, it has affected my independence. I didn't get my license until I was 22, and then I only drove freely for about 2 1/12 years. I rely on public transit, my husband, the kindness of others, and my own two legs to get around to places. This also affects my job prospects. My day partially revolves on trying to prevent myself from having seizures - don't stress too much, eat well, exercise, don't stay up too late, take meds at the same time every single day, don't do this, don't do that.

Pessimism aside, my epilepsy has pushed me out of my shell in life. Without it, I don't think I would have been on half the adventures that I've been on...

What can the average person do to help people with epilepsy? (Besides CPR & First Aid certifications)

Wow! Awesome question! :D Honestly, know how to recognize if someone is having a seizure and what to do if they are having one. This site has pretty good information on what to do.

A few quick notes: * NEVER put something in a seizing person's mouth. * NEVER hold a seizing person down. * Call 911 right away if you are unsure of what to do, especially if they have multiple seizures in a row or a seizure lasting longer than 5 minutes.

Thank you for your responses.

I have had a few seizures in my life, never diagnosed and haven't had one in 13+ years. They always involved just blacking out, distorted memory, dizziness, weakness, and general confusion.

Also, I am in university working towards a degree in Early Childhood Education and Special Education, so it is nice to be able to get information from people with all sorts of life experiences. In fact, when I was working in a Preschool a few years ago I was the only one to recognize a young child having seizures, taking care of him during and after, and providing enough information for him to ultimately being diagnosed and prescribed medication to manage his specific seizure disorder.

Again, thank you for your response. :)

Yea, it can be pretty bad if you don't (speaking from experience). The thing about epilepsy meds is that you want you keep a pretty steady therapeutic level within your body. If you are forgetting to take them, this causes the levels to dip drastically, leaving you vulnerable to seizures. Actually, forgetting your meds can leave you open to status epilepticus or SUDEP. How often do you have a seizure?

That's a bit of a tough question for me. I've had epilepsy since I was 15 (I'm 28 now). For most of this time, I've had an average of 1-2 seizures/year. However, over the past two years, I've been having about 6/year. After spending about a week in an Epilepsy Monitoring Unit about a month ago, the doctors came to the conclusion that the medication that I was on for the last few years was actually causing me more seizures. They switched me to a much more appropriate medication. So, hopefully that number will go back down to 1-2/year - or less.

Do you go to the ER after a seizure? Why or why not?

I have in the past, and it has usually been because I've had it around people who did not know what to do. And I am totally ,OK with that. I'd rather be safe than sorry. A few times I went to the hospital because I had several seizures right after another (take your seizures meds, kids!). The last time I went to the ER was back in February. I had a bad case of strep and my fever spiked pretty high and went into a seizure. My husband wanted to be safe and took me to the ER.
Thank you for doing this AMA, Do you bite your tongue while in a seizure?

Also, once you start yelling at a teenager, they stop listening to the words you're saying and start focusing on the fact that your voice is elevated.

It's not going to be easy, but you're going to need to find a good balance where you're protecting yourselves, teaching him, and not scaring him. The less yelling you do, the better... but you don't want to lose your lives in the process.

Yes that's correct! I don't want to lose our lives in the process! I hadn't read your comment thoroughly, which is why I hadn't replied. I drove around for an hour yesterday and he actually was talking and laughing at some points - good day -and driving safely!

I grew up in a snowy mountain community. My dad would take me to parking lots and make me slide. It rains a lot here, so this is a great idea of letting him slide around a parking lot a bit during one of our frequent summer storms.
This is a great idea. So many people drive dangerously in the rain and snow because they didn't have this practice.

Remain calm. Start off small. Just practising driving. Don't start till he knows how the car works. Stop. Then explain things. Keep to the side roads, for the first 10 outings. Then maybe start distances on busier roads, build it up slowly. Tell him he needs to do as you say to begin with otherwise you can't go out, trust is the key.

Don't forget: you can't stop the car, but you CAN grab the wheel. Don't panic and freeze up. Be patient and go out as much as you can and then when he has confidence in the manoeuvres etc you should then get book a single driving lesson for the instructor to evaluate him. If its no good keep practising. If he says that he's driving well and things just need tweaking, start paying for lessons then. This will save you money in the long run.

The best advice I would give is to shell out the cash for driving school. For some people teaching their kids to drive is a wonderful bonding experience that they've looked forward to for years. Where I grew up, if you were a minor, I think you were required by law to take a driver's ed class and have 10 hours of "behind the wheel" instruction with a trained driving instructor. They recommended (I think) at least 30 hours in total before the road test, but 10 with a driving instructor.

In Virginia, you have to have 7 hours with an instructor driving and 7 hours with an instructor observing, plus 45 - read that again 45!, hours with your parent or sibling driving. They make you fill out a log and chronicle all the driving you do. It is long and painful, but the gist of it is they want these teen drivers to be better.

My parents hired a pro for 2 hours to show me the basics. I think that helped a lot because they weren't there for the first dumb thoughts/mistakes. I also felt comfortable asking all my stupid questions to a stranger who specializes in it then to my parents. Goof0d luck, and stay calm.

take him to large, empty parking lots many times so he's fully comfortable with handling the car and understanding it's boundaries. Also for the long term: seriously consider putting him into a racing school. There he will really learn how to drive a car at its limits: this translates to being a better driver day-to-day. I have take a few driving courses when i was in my later teens, and have logged many hours on the track with my dad's auto club (when i was 18 thru 24 years old) and I feel I'm a better daily driver for it. With this kind of experience under his belt, he is less likely to make a noob mistake during an emergency and crash the car; added benefit is taking the driving course is damn fun!

My little brother recently received his learners permit, so I've been driving around with him.

First, we just drove around the neighborhood then back roads. Once he got more confident we took a long drive down a low traffic highway. Once he felt really comfortable with the car and the road we started on getting him more comfortable with other drivers.

The two main tips I'm giving him, give everyone a wide buffer and assume everyone before you and behind is an asshole and about to do something dumb at any moment. Second, is to drive a mile ahead of you and a mile behind so you are not surprised by any changes in traffic or yours surrounding.

He's doing great, holding the speed limit like gospel and drives casually.
I'm taking him out now for another session. Thanks for all of your tips! This was my first post ever!

Drive yourself to empty car lots, and make him practice there until he his comfortable. Have him turn into a parking space without touching the lines. If the lot is wide enough, use parking spots as lanes. Make sure he checks his blind spot when you have him changing lanes, this is a habit he absolutely needs to develop. Have him accelerate to as fast as the space in the lot allows him, then make him brake with the pedal to the floor, so he gets used to the distance he needs to stop. Stress the importance of keeping his distances. If he ever has troubles driving in a straight line and keeps adjusting, tell him to look further on the road.

I spent a lot of time on tractors and go karts before i drove a car for the first time when i was 12. I think all of those things helped a lot for when it was time to actually start driving.

There is no replacement for hours. Start slow. Let him get used to things one at a time. My dad used to make little obstacle courses for me to do slalom through, then tight corners that required me to position correctly first, then an imaginary parking spot that i couldn't see the front of. I didn't realize for years how useful that was until the first time i drove a truck.

My dad taught me to parallel park using large appliance boxes and a bucket to represent where the wheel of the car you are parking behind would be (to line up your car's back wheel up). It worked like a charm and I can still parallel park really well (in my 30s).

I learned the rules of driving from youtube and the dmv booklet. Got a grasp of the car by getting hours driving around an empty parking lot. Mainly acceleration and braking. I've already spent years riding a bicycle nearby cars, wasnt difficult for me to actually drive one. Freeway was no different.

I'm using the dmv book. It's really helpful to know what are the actual reference points. I've been driving for so long that it is so natural, that I'm not sure what the reference points I'm using. Currently teaching my 15 year old to drive. There's a lot of good advice on here already but one that I see missing or I overlooked; be courteous to other drivers and pedestrians. The most proud moment I've had with him driving, the one that made me go "I think I'm doing alright here", was when he stopped for someone crossing the road even though he didn't have to. They learn a lot more than you realize from having watched you, so try to relax and let him show you what he's learned already. The key is the relax part, he can't if you aren't.

We've actually hit 11 hrs of practice driving yesterday. It's not like I'm yelling all the time, I just yelled stop yesterday 1x and he was angry about that, but we continued to drive for 2 hours, so we both got over it.

Tip #1: Don't Panic.

Tip #2: Take him to a more deserted area or deserted parking lot for practice, either initially or occasionally. It is a lot less stressful for both starting out where there are less obstacles.

Try to be as passive as possible. Don't open your mouth unless there's an imminent threat. He probably knows he's not good, you don't have to point out everything. You can make comments later.

(The first time I drove, my dad just picked me up from school and said, "ok, now drive home." It was scary, but he didn't say much which gave me a lot of confidence.)

If his school offers drivers ed sign him up and let them deal with that stress.

I jumped in my mom's car and aced the driving portion of my test with less than 30 minutes behind the wheel. I was scared of driving. The thought of pushing a ton or two of explosiony metal down the road at 50mph was a lot to be responsible for. I believe I owe it to simply watching my mother's driving habits. Feeling for when she began to brake and at what speed we were driving. He's obviously a bit ahead of where I was, but it can't hurt to talk about what you are doing while driving with him. Asking him if he feels you engaging the brake, and asking him why you do engage it when you do. Ask him to pretend he was driving and talk about where his eyes would and should be. Make sure he is noticing the impatient drivers looking to turn onto the road you are on. Make sure he should assume every one will pull out at the worst time, as if oblivious to your presence. Quiz him on how fast you are driving without him seeing the speedometer.

If you can drive a manual pick up truck safely in the city then you can handle an automatic easily. it was this kind of training that allowed me to drive 4 states away at 18 to go to the beach and my parents didnt have to worry too much because they knew I could handle myself.
